beats.label: Trading places — the seesaw
beats.prompt: a witch and a scientist trading places on a seesaw while a crowd below cheers
beats.vo: It's not a coincidence that two things often trade places in public opinion and in reality.

beats.label: Science's battle cry
beats.prompt: an army in white lab coats marching with banners, shouting one battle cry, trampling little charms underfoot
beats.vo: If science had a battle cry, it would be stop all this nonsense, folkism, superstition, and the ever formidable woo. We've put up with nonsense for far too long.

beats.label: The empty magician's hat
beats.prompt: a magician's hat turned upside down and shaken empty over a bare stone table
beats.vo: Now it's time to stop all this hocus pocus and face the facts. Matter is matter and that's all we've got.

beats.label: A young woman in a male world
beats.prompt: a young woman standing very straight in a lecture hall full of suited men, dark ink soaking up through her from the floor
beats.vo: And I, as a young woman in a male world wanting so badly to be respected, not to be one of those who believed in silly things like magic and God, accepted this ill-gotten premonition into every pore till it oozed out.

beats.label: Candles for a lightbulb
beats.prompt: frightened villagers trading their candles to a salesman for one glowing lightbulb
beats.vo: We had magic because we were scared. We couldn't explain everything. Now we have science so we don't need magic anymore. And anyone who thinks we do is stupid and wrong.

beats.label: The beautiful method — glass sieves
beats.prompt: a beautiful glass machine of funnels and sieves straining a muddy river into one clear drop
beats.vo: But here's where things get tricky because science doesn't have a battle cry because it's not really an it, instead it's a method, a way of conducting experiments that eliminates as many variables as possible.

beats.label: One thing known for sure
beats.prompt: a woman holding up one tiny glowing crystal in a vast darkness
beats.vo: In theory, it's rather beautiful. The idea that we could, the idea that we, the idea that we could know something, even one thing for sure, gets more and more magnificent the longer you think about it.

beats.label: A cathedral of knowledge
beats.prompt: glass blocks stacking themselves into a towering cathedral
beats.vo: And the harder you realize it is to know anything, anything at all. And then that all this knowledge could build up on itself and form these coherent systems.

beats.label: The balcony proclamation
beats.prompt: scientists in white coats proclaiming from a balcony to a cheering crowd
beats.vo: We did a study, say scientists in white coats in labs somewhere, in some lab somewhere, and now we know this thing.

beats.label: Drink more water
beats.prompt: a person happily drinking from a glass of water taller than they are
beats.vo: Sometimes it's just common sense. It turns out drinking more water is actually really good for you and for all these various reasons. So everyone should do it a lot.

beats.label: A staircase into the clouds
beats.prompt: a staircase of stepping stones rising into the clouds, people climbing it single file
beats.vo: But we know it's just one step in a long chain of steps and that we're getting closer to knowing everything.

beats.label: Manna from the sky
beats.prompt: nuggets of gold raining gently from the sky while people below catch them in baskets
beats.vo: In fact, they could say almost anything. And I, like most people, would believe it, delivering these nuggets of truth and wisdom that we no longer have to worry about, like manna from the sky.

beats.label: Dinner with the PhD student
beats.prompt: a candlelit dinner date, the student leaning across the table to whisper
beats.vo: The first time I really questioned this system was when I dated a PhD student at UCLA.

beats.label: The advisor tips the scales
beats.prompt: an advisor secretly tipping a great brass scale in a dark laboratory at night
beats.vo: And he mentioned casually in passing that all their numbers were wrong. Evidently, his advisor had been fudging the numbers for years.

beats.label: Seven years — a fork in the road
beats.prompt: a student standing at a fork in a long road, looking back at seven milestones behind him
beats.vo: Now, seven years into his PhD, he was faced with a moral conundrum. I'll spare you the conclusion or any of the names involved.

beats.label: Reading The Blank Slate at night
beats.prompt: a woman reading an enormous thick book by lamplight in the middle of the night, giggling
beats.vo: In a rather dark hour, I read almost the entirety of Steven Pinker's The Blank Slate, a devout atheist. I was almost giggling to myself when I read the chapter on the various causes of our personality as children.

beats.label: The last puzzle piece glows
beats.prompt: a jigsaw puzzle almost finished, the last piece glowing and refusing to fit
beats.vo: He goes into great detail, explaining the common non-influences that have proven to have no effect—parents, images, and the media—but makes it clear that there is 10% of inexplicables that cannot be explained in any one way.

beats.label: Identical twins, different shadows
beats.prompt: identical twins standing side by side, casting two different shadows
beats.vo: Even in identical twins, they differ from birth in this mysterious 10th percentage.

beats.label: The soul rising from the book
beats.prompt: a small glowing soul rising out of an open book while its author looks away, pretending not to notice
beats.vo: Given my aforementioned desperate fear of even suggesting something supernatural, I was almost embarrassed on his account for how strongly this suggested the existence of a soul. And yet, somehow, he confidently finished the chapter without giving any additional explanation for this now most mysterious 10% of ambiguity.

beats.label: Every door opens on stars
beats.prompt: a woman opening door after door in a long hallway, a starry sky pouring out of each one
beats.vo: Is it just me, or does every new bit of science we uncover prove, more and more, the existence of magic and of God?

beats.label: The double slit and the eye
beats.prompt: a beam of light splitting into ripples through two slits while a giant eye watches from above
beats.vo: I came across a YouTube short the other day saying they did an experiment—a second version of the slit experiment—in which they decided whether to observe after the fact, and particles behaved as waves or particles depending on whether they decided to observe it after the

beats.label: Time runs backwards
beats.prompt: clocks melting and spinning backwards around a shrugging woman
beats.vo: Meaning, while I'm not entirely sure what it means, that time travel is possible?

beats.label: Rockefeller ransacks the herb garden
beats.prompt: a tycoon in a top hat ransacking a grandmother's herb garden, stuffing plants into a money bag
beats.vo: After Rockefeller casually ransacked our age-old herbalism tradition in favor of newer and more modern and better ones, scientists have been discovering the health benefits of things like turmeric and St. John's wort.

beats.label: The golden thread pulled from the tapestry
beats.prompt: tweezers pulling one golden thread out of a whole tapestry as the tapestry goes dim
beats.vo: What I find especially worth noting is that turmeric works best as a whole plant, when taken with animal fat and pepper. However, scientists, in their infinite pursuit of specificity, have disentangled the active compound curcumin from the plant, making it less effective.

beats.label: The willow gives its bark
beats.prompt: a willow tree by a river handing down a strip of its bark to an outstretched hand
beats.vo: Similarly, white willow bark, from which is derived salicylic acid, the active compound in aspirin, manages to steer clear of things like stomach ulcers, the side effects of aspirin, when taken as a whole plant.

beats.label: The wildflower lifts her out
beats.prompt: a yellow wildflower gently lifting a person out of a dark pit
beats.vo: And St. John's wort, a naturally occurring SSRI, is much easier to get off of than, say, Prozac.

beats.label: The brother and the magnifying glass
beats.prompt: a man squinting at a potted plant through a magnifying glass while the plant patiently waits
beats.vo: My brother, a hard-minded materialist, agrees that plants might have amazing healing potential, but he just wishes scientists would have more time to study them. That would be nice, wouldn't it? To be able to name all the chemicals before we put them in our body?

beats.label: The tangled web of compounds
beats.prompt: a vast tangled web of glowing threads connecting thousands of seeds, one person trying to trace a single thread
beats.vo: The problem, I think, is the sheer number of compounds, not to mention their interactions.
